title: Pride and Prejudice
author: Jane Austen
openingText: It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife. However little known the feelings or views of such a man may be on his first entering a neighbourhood, this truth is so well fixed in the minds of the surrounding families, that he is considered the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters.
about:
Pride and Prejudice is the story of Elizabeth Bennet — second of five sisters in a country gentleman's family — and her gradual change of mind about the wealthy, proud Mr. Darcy. The plot turns on misunderstandings, letters, and chance encounters; the prose is comic, sharp, and almost surgically observed. The novel was published in 1813 and has been continuously in print ever since.

Jane Austen wrote it in her late twenties. It was her second novel and made her name. Austen's particular form — the marriage plot used as a vehicle for moral and social analysis — is already fully developed here; this is the most polished version of it. The novel is funnier than its reputation suggests, and harder. It is also a serious portrait of how marriage decisions worked under real economic constraint, which most film adaptations soften.

angleCards.title: Intelligence as the only real virtue.
angleCards.text: The novel consistently rewards characters who see clearly and punishes those who perform. I want to read it as Austen's sustained argument that good judgement — not wealth, not rank, not even kindness — is the one quality that makes a person worth marrying.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Pride and Prejudice as Austen's argument that intelligence and honesty are the only real romantic virtues — and that every other quality the world prizes (money, status, manners) is secondary or dangerous.

angleCards.title: The stakes of the marriage market.
angleCards.text: Elizabeth Bennet is funny and smart and entirely at the mercy of men she can't control. A wrong marriage means a wasted life; no marriage means poverty. I want to read the comedy without losing sight of what is actually at stake for every woman in every scene.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the marriage market — what it actually meant to be a woman in 1813 with no economic independence — and understand the constraints that make every choice in the novel carry real weight.

angleCards.title: Darcy's humiliation as education.
angleCards.text: He is rich, handsome, well-connected, and entirely wrong about himself. His first proposal to Elizabeth is one of the great literary disasters. I want to track exactly what it takes to break his pride — and whether Austen presents that transformation as realistic.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Darcy's arc — a man with every advantage who has to learn that his advantages mean nothing without humility — and ask what Austen thinks it actually takes for a proud person to change.

angleCards.title: Elizabeth as unreliable narrator of her own life.
angleCards.text: She is witty and self-aware — and badly wrong about Wickham, wrong about Darcy, wrong about Jane's feelings. I want to read the novel asking where Elizabeth's self-knowledge fails her, and whether Austen intends her as a cautionary tale as much as a heroine.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to ask whether Elizabeth Bennet is the most psychologically realistic character in 19th century fiction — testing her against the novel's events to see whether she is as perceptive as she believes herself to be.

cast.name: Elizabeth Bennet
cast.description: The second of five sisters, Austen's most beloved heroine, and the sharpest mind in the room — except when her own feelings are involved. Her wit is real, her judgement is mostly sound, and her errors are precisely calibrated to teach her something she couldn't have learned any other way.

cast.name: Mr. Darcy
cast.description: Wealthy, handsome, and socially impeccable — and so convinced of his own superiority that he insults Elizabeth in their first meeting and then can't stop thinking about her. His arc is the novel's argument that genuine self-knowledge requires a catastrophic failure of self-image.

cast.name: Jane Bennet
cast.description: Elizabeth's elder sister: beautiful, genuinely kind, and constitutionally unable to think badly of anyone. Her goodness is real but costly — it makes her unreadable and nearly loses her the man who loves her. Austen admires her and also gently shows what pure benevolence cannot protect you from.

cast.name: Mr. Wickham
cast.description: The handsome militia officer who wins everyone's sympathy in the first hour and is believed unreservedly for months. He is the novel's argument that charm without character is indistinguishable from virtue — until the consequences arrive.

cast.name: Mrs. Bennet
cast.description: Nervy, tactical, and frequently embarrassing — but also, quietly, correct about the stakes. Getting her daughters married is her only lever on the world. Austen makes her ridiculous and also makes sure we feel exactly why she is like this.

cast.name: Mr. Collins
cast.description: The clergyman who will inherit the Bennet estate and arrives to marry one of the daughters as a kind of charitable act. His pomposity is so total that he cannot perceive rejection. He is the novel's purest comic creation and its most pointed comment on how class produces moral blindness.

acclaim.quote: That young lady had a talent for describing the involvements and feelings and characters of ordinary life which is to me the most wonderful I ever met with.

whyItMatters.title: The Marriage Plot as Argument
whyItMatters.body: Pride and Prejudice uses the question of who marries whom as a way of examining what people are actually like — how they reveal themselves under courtship, money pressure, and family scrutiny. The novel argues that you can know a person, and that knowing them well enough is what marriage requires.

whyItMatters.title: Comedy as a Moral Tool
whyItMatters.body: Austen's wit is not decoration. It is how the novel does its analytical work. The comedy lands hardest on people who are wrong about themselves — vain, deluded, performing virtues they do not have. Reading Austen sharpens your eye for the same patterns in life.

whyItMatters.title: Money Underneath Everything
whyItMatters.body: The novel never lets you forget what marriages were economically. Mr. Bennet's estate is entailed away from his daughters. They have nothing. Everyone in the novel knows this and acts accordingly. The romance works because the economic pressure is real.
